props.title: The French Lieutenant's Woman
props.initialSlug: A Victorian love affair haunts its modern retelling

sections.content: The French Lieutenant's Woman brilliantly interweaves two parallel love stories through an innovative dual-narrative structure. Meryl Streep and Jeremy Irons each play two roles - Victorian-era lovers and modern actors performing those same characters. This adaptation of John Fowles' novel pioneered meta-storytelling techniques that influenced later films like Adaptation (2002) and The Hours (2002). Harold Pinter's screenplay masterfully parallels the constraints of Victorian society with contemporary relationship dynamics, while Karel Reisz's direction seamlessly transitions between timeframes through precise visual matching.

sections.content: The film's groundbreaking structure influenced a wave of meta-fictional period dramas that examined how we relate to historical narratives. Orlando (1992) similarly plays with time periods and gender roles, while The Piano (1993) echoes the themes of forbidden passion and societal restrictions in Victorian-era New Zealand. The technique of parallel storytelling across time periods later emerged in works like The Hours (2002) and Cloud Atlas (2012).

Karel Reisz's meticulous direction emphasizes the power dynamics of Victorian society through carefully composed frames and purposeful camera movements. The film's cinematography by Freddie Francis creates striking visual contrasts between the harsh Dorset coastline and the ornate interiors, reminiscent of other period masterworks like Barry Lyndon (1975) and The Draughtsman's Contract (1982). sections.content: The film's influence extends beyond its narrative structure to its treatment of feminist themes and social criticism. Like later works such as The Piano (1993) and The Governess (1998), it presents a complex female protagonist who defies Victorian conventions. Streep's nuanced dual performance established a template for actresses navigating period and contemporary scenes, later seen in films like The Hours (2002) and Julie & Julia (2009).
